{"claims":[{"id":"c1","text":"In regulated deployment, a control protocol becomes part of a wider oversight system (model validation, internal audit, supervisory reporting, incident management, board accountability). Pricing the control tax therefore requires attention to that system: Layer 2, institutional embedding, and not only Layer 1, protocol design.","methods":["Two-layer framing (protocol design vs institutional embedding)","Literature synthesis across AI control, scalable oversight, sovereign AI, compute governance and structural asymmetry","Illustrative stress scenario feeding monitor flags into incident management"],"results":["Three recurring distinctions: monitoring vs acting on monitoring; detecting vs explaining; improving safety vs preserving usefulness","Stress scenario: a monitor flag leads to operations triage, then the model risk function, case-record review, a vendor ticket, scope-narrowing and regulator-notification decisions"],"conditions":["Applies to regulated deployers that consume vendor models via API or managed endpoints"]},{"id":"c2","text":"The AI stack can be described for a regulated deployer through four layers: data, model, infrastructure and interaction. An import-dependent deployer typically retains its own data, lacks model access, has partial infrastructure access, and has interaction access that depends on its own application architecture.","methods":["Adaptation of the four-pillar sovereign-AI framework, replacing the operational pillar with an interaction layer (prompts, outputs, tool calls, records)","Access audit in the payments case"],"results":["Typical access: weights, architecture and activations are vendor-held; serving uses a foreign-operated cloud region, sometimes with a residency rider","Case audit: Data shared, Model vendor-led, Infrastructure shared, Interaction operator-led"],"conditions":["Offered as a descriptive aid, not a settled taxonomy"]},{"id":"c3","text":"For a regulated deployer, the practical questions raised by control protocols are largely organisational: who calibrates the monitor, who reviews flags, how behaviour is documented, and cost and latency.","methods":["Protocol-considerations table","Protocol feasibility discussion in the case"],"results":["Output monitoring: calibration and documentation, thresholds justified to model risk","Activation-level monitoring needs scarce specialist expertise","Defer-to-trusted: workflow and customer-treatment design","Resampling: cost and latency against service levels","Human audit: staffing and escalation","Weights patching is handled through the vendor","Operator treats activation-level and interpretability monitoring as longer-term possibilities"],"conditions":["Model access is absent under API or managed endpoints"]},{"id":"c4","text":"The realised control tax equals instrumented-control cost plus sovereignty discount cost, where the latter is an informal umbrella for procurement, legal and vendor-management frictions that overlap third-party risk management. Oversight costs tend to shift between budget lines rather than disappear.","methods":["Conceptual decomposition (not an accounting identity)","Four spend categories in the case: contractual, architectural, capacity, scope decisions"],"results":["Control tax is expected to be experienced as an extension of existing third-party and model risk budgets","Relying on vendor attestations lowers validation effort but raises contract management","Narrowing scope lowers monitoring effort but raises manual processing"],"conditions":["Sovereignty discount is not operationalised or estimated by the simulator"]},{"id":"c5","text":"The paper adopts Position C (calibrated or bounded control) as a working frame, because Positions A (safety-maximalist) and B (sovereignty-maximalist) are not actionable on relevant timescales. It guides oversight with a six-consideration rubric that is not a weighted formula.","methods":["Comparison of three positions","Six considerations: severity and reversibility, protocol maturity, vendor concentration, absorptive capacity, cost vs value, coalition paths"],"results":["A implies abstention from committed deployments; B implies capability investment many states cannot make this decade","Against strong A: deployers already govern uninspectable services","Against strong B: proportionate oversight can do meaningful work","Pax Silica is cited as evidence that supply may be tied to political alignment"],"conditions":["Weights of the considerations vary by sector and remain an open question"]},{"id":"c6","text":"A synthetic payments-dispute simulation environment provides reusable tooling and construct validation. It is not real-world evidence, and no quantitative conclusions are drawn from it.","methods":["20 curated access profiles, 10 protocols, 3 agents (honest, careless, stealthy access-aware), thresholds 0.35/0.55/0.75, audit budgets 2%/5%/20%, 5 seeds, 50 cases per condition","Catastrophic classes C1 to C4 as labels","Unitless decomposed cost proxy"],"results":["27,000 condition rows and 1,350,000 case simulations completed, with all metrics produced","No causal attribution to individual settings because configurations are curated, not full-factorial","Scripted access-aware agent is far weaker than a capable red team","No sovereignty-discount estimates reported"],"conditions":["Human factors and institutional overheads are not modelled","A full-factorial design is supported by the code"]},{"id":"c7","text":"Evaluation for regulated settings should report prevention, diagnosis, usefulness and cost together. Joint safety-plus-usefulness targets guard against counting usefulness loss, for example from scope restriction, as a free safety gain.","methods":["Metric set including task success, failure by class, diagnosis success and cost proxy","Target-reachability template (≤1% failure and ≥75% usefulness)","Minimum task-success variant of the threshold utility","Safety-usefulness-cost frontier"],"results":["Scope restriction trades capability for safety","No single protocol should be presented as a complete answer","Diagnosis is treated as a first-class outcome alongside prevention"],"conditions":["The reachability table is a template, not findings"]},{"id":"c8","text":"In the anonymised national payments case, catastrophic actions rank by severity C1 < C2 < C3 < C4. Payments is comparatively favourable terrain for oversight, so the case does not straightforwardly generalise to other sectors.","methods":["Illustrative case interpretation","Generalisability discussion"],"results":["C1: individual hold or release; C2: systematic mis-triage propagating across cases; C3: exposure of protected data; C4: disturbing settlement","Favourable because catastrophes are crisp, tool surfaces can be narrowed, and incident management is mature","Healthcare, public administration and enterprise may have fuzzier catastrophes and wider action surfaces"],"conditions":["Descriptive framework is sector-agnostic; the case is not"]}],
"items":[
{"id":"q1","type":"failure","claims":["c8","c7"],"pair":null,"question":"The payments case treats excluding C4-adjacent action paths as a manageable scope decision. Would scope restriction remain as workable an oversight lever in a general enterprise deployment, and why?","answer":"Probably not as workable. Scope restriction relies on a narrowable tool surface and a crisp definition of catastrophic actions, both of which the paper cites as features of payments. Enterprise deployments may have wide action surfaces and fuzzy catastrophe definitions, so it is harder to know which actions to exclude without losing much usefulness.","rubric":["Says scope restriction would be less workable / harder to apply","Reason: it depends on narrowable tool surfaces and/or crisply defined catastrophes, which enterprise settings may lack"]},
{"id":"q2","type":"failure","claims":["c1","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Under what organisational condition would adding the human audit protocol on top of an output monitor add little real oversight, and why?","answer":"It would add little when the organisation lacks the staffing or escalation paths to review flagged cases in time. The paper stresses that a flag has value only if there is a process for acting on it, and that human audit depends on review budget and the timeliness of escalation.","rubric":["Identifies insufficient review capacity, staffing, or escalation process as the condition","Reason: monitoring has value only if flagged cases are acted on (monitoring vs acting distinction / audit capacity dependence)"]},
{"id":"q3","type":"failure","claims":["c6","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Suppose a user's run of the environment showed complete I/O logs improving diagnosis success. Would that gain carry over to a real institution whose staff lack the expertise to review the logs, and why?","answer":"No, it would not necessarily carry over. The simulator does not model human factors, and the paper notes that records retained but never reviewed, or misread by staff without expertise, contribute little to oversight.","rubric":["Says the gain would not (reliably) carry over","Reason: the environment does not model human capacity to use records, and unreviewed or misinterpreted logs add little oversight"]},
{"id":"q4","type":"failure","claims":["c1","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"If a deployer validates its vendor model once before go-live, when would that validation stop supporting its model risk obligations, and why?","answer":"It stops being reliable when the model is unpinned and the vendor changes it on its own schedule. Model risk practice assumes validating and monitoring a specific model, so an unannounced update leaves the validated object no longer the one in production.","rubric":["Identifies vendor model updates under unpinned (or un-notified) version control as the condition","Reason: validation applies to a specific model version, so changes on the vendor's schedule invalidate it"]},
{"id":"q5","type":"failure","claims":["c3","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"Would the resampling protocol remain attractive for the Operator's dispute triage if dispute-handling deadlines were very tight, and why?","answer":"It would be less attractive. Resampling generates additional candidate actions, which adds model queries, cost and latency. That conflicts with throughput and with scheme-rule or regulatory timelines for dispute handling.","rubric":["Says it would be less attractive / problematic","Reason: extra queries add latency and cost that conflict with service-level or scheme-rule deadlines"]},
{"id":"q6","type":"failure","claims":["c6","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"In a configuration where vendor support is set to none, would the vendor escalation protocol be expected to improve diagnosis, and why?","answer":"No. Vendor escalation works by requesting delayed or guaranteed vendor support for diagnosis or attestation, and the paper says protocols relying on vendor support depend on its terms and responsiveness. With no support available, there is nothing to escalate to.","rubric":["Says no / little improvement expected","Reason: the protocol's effect depends on available vendor support terms, which are absent"]},
{"id":"q7","type":"why","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does the size of the run (27,000 condition rows) not allow the paper to estimate the effect of the pre-execution gateway?","answer":"The 20 access profiles were curated to span many arrangements, not varied one factor at a time. The gateway setting is therefore confounded with other settings. More seeds, thresholds or cases add replication, not identification, so a full-factorial design would be needed.","rubric":["States that the configurations are curated, not full-factorial, so gateway is confounded with other factors","Notes that more rows or replications do not fix this design limitation"]},
{"id":"q8","type":"why","claims":["c2","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Why is it useful for this paper's purposes to replace the operational pillar with an interaction layer when adapting the four-pillar framework?","answer":"The interaction layer (prompts, outputs, tool calls, records) is where an import-dependent deployer actually has control: the Operator's interaction layer is operator-led while the model is vendor-led. It is also where deployable controls such as gateways, logging and output monitoring sit, so the layer captures the deployer's main lever for oversight.","rubric":["Says the interaction layer is the one the deployer controls (e.g., operator-led vs vendor-led model)","Links it to where implementable controls such as logging, gateway, and output monitoring reside"]},
{"id":"q9","type":"why","claims":["c5","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"Under the balancing framework, why would C4 justify more oversight investment than C1 in the payments case?","answer":"Severity and reversibility is the first consideration. C1 is a bounded, reversible error on one transaction, whereas C4 can disturb settlement, a systemic and hard-to-reverse failure. Higher severity and lower reversibility justify greater oversight.","rubric":["States C4 warrants more oversight","Reason: C1 is bounded and reversible while C4 is systemic or irreversible, per the severity/reversibility consideration"]},
{"id":"q10","type":"why","claims":["c2","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Why is activation-level trusted monitoring especially hard for the Operator, beyond the shortage of specialist skills?","answer":"The Operator's access audit shows the model layer is vendor-led, and under managed-endpoint access activations are vendor-held. The internal signals the protocol needs are therefore not available to the Operator without the vendor.","rubric":["Points to lack of model access: activations or internal signals are vendor-held under API or managed endpoint","Connects this to the model layer being vendor-led in the case"]},
{"id":"q11","type":"why","claims":["c6","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"Why is the macro-shutdown protocol particularly suited to the C2 failure class rather than C1?","answer":"Macro-shutdown acts on clusters after repeated suspiciousness, and C2 is by definition a systematic mis-triage pattern across a case cluster. Per-case checks may let each individual error pass while the pattern propagates, whereas C1 is a single-case error.","rubric":["Says macro-shutdown matches C2","Reason: it operates on clusters / repeated signals, and C2 is a cross-case pattern rather than an individual error"]},
{"id":"q12","type":"why","claims":["c8","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does the stress scenario of a slow elevation in hold recommendations for one merchant category represent a C2 risk rather than a C1 risk?","answer":"The concern is a systematic pattern spread across many cases in a category that builds before detection, which matches C2's definition. C1 concerns an incorrect hold or release on a single transaction.","rubric":["Identifies it as C2","Reason: it is a pattern across many cases propagating before detection, not a single-case error"]},
{"id":"q13","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c6"],"pair":"p1","question":"If the number of random seeds in the large run were doubled to 10, would the number of aggregate condition rows change?","answer":"Yes. Seeds are a factor in the condition grid, so rows would double from 27,000 to 54,000, and case simulations would double to 2.7 million.","rubric":["Says yes, rows change","Gives 54,000 rows (or explains seeds multiply the condition count)"]},
{"id":"q14","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c6"],"pair":"p1","question":"If the number of synthetic cases per condition in the large run were doubled to 100, would the number of aggregate condition rows change?","answer":"No. Cases per condition are aggregated within each row, so the row count stays at 27,000. Only case simulations rise, to 2.7 million.","rubric":["Says no, rows stay at 27,000","Reason: cases are within-condition; only the simulation count (2.7M) changes"]},
{"id":"q15","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2","c3","c8"],"pair":"p2","question":"Under the Operator's access arrangement in the case, is output-level trusted monitoring feasible for the Operator to implement in-house?","answer":"Yes. It scores outputs and actions, which flow through the Operator-led interaction layer. The main requirements are calibration, documentation and validation through existing model risk processes.","rubric":["Says yes, feasible","Reason: it relies on outputs in the operator-controlled interaction layer, needing calibration and documentation rather than model access"]},
{"id":"q16","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2","c3","c8"],"pair":"p2","question":"Under the Operator's access arrangement in the case, is trace/activation-level trusted monitoring feasible for the Operator to implement in-house?","answer":"No. It needs internal model signals, which are vendor-held under the managed endpoint, plus scarce expertise. The Operator would treat it as a longer-term possibility dependent on the vendor's roadmap.","rubric":["Says no, not feasible in-house now","Reason: activations are vendor-held (model layer vendor-led) and/or specialist expertise is lacking"]},
{"id":"q17","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c7"],"pair":"p3","question":"In the target-reachability analysis, would a profile that achieves 0.5% failure by restricting scope so that usefulness falls to 60% count as reaching the target?","answer":"No. The target jointly requires ≤1% failure and ≥75% usefulness, and 60% usefulness fails the second condition despite the low failure rate.","rubric":["Says no","Reason: usefulness of 60% is below the 75% requirement of the joint target"]},
{"id":"q18","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c7"],"pair":"p3","question":"In the target-reachability analysis, would a profile with 0.8% failure and 80% usefulness count as reaching the target?","answer":"Yes. It meets both conditions: failure is at or below 1% and usefulness is at or above 75%.","rubric":["Says yes","Reason: satisfies both ≤1% failure and ≥75% usefulness"]},
{"id":"q19","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c4"],"pair":"p4","question":"In the paper's decomposition of the realised control tax, would the cost of additional legal review of vendor contracts fall under sovereignty discount cost?","answer":"Yes. Legal review and procurement frictions arising from reliance on externally supplied AI are exactly what the informal sovereignty discount umbrella covers.","rubric":["Says yes, sovereignty discount cost","Reason: it is an institutional or contractual friction from vendor reliance, not a protocol-level cost"]},
{"id":"q20","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c4","c6"],"pair":"p4","question":"In the paper's decomposition of the realised control tax, would the cost of extra monitor calls per case fall under sovereignty discount cost?","answer":"No. Monitor calls are protocol-level costs of the control mechanism itself, which belong to instrumented-control cost; the simulator's proxy captures them as monitoring cost.","rubric":["Says no, it is instrumented-control cost","Reason: it is a protocol-level monitoring cost (as in the simulator's cost proxy), not an institutional friction"]},
{"id":"q21","type":"transfer","claims":["c5","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Of two deployers, one facing a single viable frontier-model vendor and one facing several substitutable vendors, which is better placed to secure terms that make the vendor escalation protocol useful, and why?","answer":"The deployer with several substitutable vendors. Vendor concentration affects bargaining power over terms of supply, such as guaranteed support. Vendor escalation's usefulness depends on those terms and on the vendor's responsiveness.","rubric":["Chooses the deployer with several vendors","Reason: greater bargaining power yields better support terms, on which vendor escalation depends"]},
{"id":"q22","type":"transfer","claims":["c5","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Several small payment operators in one jurisdiction each cannot afford staff able to interpret monitor outputs. Which considerations in the balancing framework point to a remedy, and what is it?","answer":"Absorptive capacity identifies the problem: oversight is useful only if someone can interpret monitor outputs. Coalition paths offer the remedy: shared audit consortia or regional arrangements amortise the cost of oversight capability across deployers.","rubric":["Proposes a coalition path (e.g., shared audit consortium) to pool capability","Links it to the absorptive-capacity concern and/or cost amortisation across deployers"]},
{"id":"q23","type":"transfer","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"If a user reran the large-run configuration adding a fourth monitor threshold (0.95), keeping everything else the same, how many condition rows and case simulations would result?","answer":"20 × 10 × 3 × 4 × 3 × 5 gives 36,000 condition rows. At 50 cases each, that is 1,800,000 case simulations.","rubric":["Gives 36,000 condition rows","Gives 1,800,000 case simulations"]},
{"id":"q24","type":"transfer","claims":["c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Under the paper's framework, how much oversight investment should a deployer give a vendor model that only drafts internal, easily corrected notes, and why?","answer":"Relatively light oversight. The possible errors are low-severity and reversible, and the cost-versus-value consideration recognises that some use cases do not justify heavy monitoring and audit regimes.","rubric":["Says light / proportionately low oversight","Reason: low severity and high reversibility, and/or oversight cost should be weighed against use-case value"]},
{"id":"q25","type":"transfer","claims":["c2","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"A regulated deployer runs an open-weight model on its own in-jurisdiction hardware. Which protocols in the paper's protocol table that the Operator lacked become available in principle, and what constraint still remains?","answer":"With model access, activation-level monitoring and in-house weights patching become possible rather than vendor-mediated. However, interpreting internal signals still needs specialist expertise that is scarce in regulated institutions.","rubric":["Names activation/trace-level monitoring and/or in-house weights patching as newly feasible","Notes the remaining constraint of scarce specialist expertise"]},
{"id":"q26","type":"transfer","claims":["c7","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"A team adds a protocol to the environment that blocks all recommend_hold and recommend_release actions. How should they report it so the result is not misleading, and why?","answer":"They should report usefulness or task success, and ideally a joint target with a minimum task-success requirement, alongside failure. Blocking those actions will cut failures largely by disabling useful work, which a failure-only report would count as a free safety gain.","rubric":["Recommends reporting usefulness / a joint safety-plus-usefulness target (or minimum task-success variant), not failure alone","Reason: disabling actions lowers failure trivially by sacrificing useful work"]},
{"id":"q27","type":"transfer","claims":["c4","c7"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployer tells its regulator that narrowing an AI assistant's scope reduced both failures and monitoring costs. What should the regulator ask about to test the efficiency claim, and why?","answer":"The regulator should ask about forgone usefulness and the added manual processing for excluded actions. The paper argues that oversight costs are typically shifted rather than eliminated, and narrowing scope lowers monitoring effort but raises manual processing.","rubric":["Asks about manual processing burden and/or lost usefulness","Reason: costs shift between budget lines rather than disappear"]},
{"id":"q28","type":"connect","claims":["c2","c3","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"If the case's access audit had found the interaction layer vendor-led rather than operator-led, which of the paper's feasibility conclusions about the Operator would be undermined?","answer":"The conclusion that the Operator can implement output monitoring, defer-to-trusted routing, gateways, record-keeping and escalation through its own application and governance machinery. Those rely on the Operator designing and operating the surrounding workflow and case records.","rubric":["Identifies the Operator's ability to implement application-level controls (output monitoring, gateway, logging, defer-to-trusted) in-house","Reason: these depend on operator control of the interaction layer and workflow"]},
{"id":"q29","type":"connect","claims":["c5"],"pair":null,"question":"If regulated deployers had no existing practices for governing technology services whose internals they cannot inspect, which of the paper's arguments would lose its support?","answer":"The argument against a strong reading of Position A. That rebuttal rests on deployers already managing uninspectable services, into whose governance partial-assurance control protocols could be incorporated.","rubric":["Names the rebuttal of (strong) Position A / safety-maximalism","Reason: it relies on existing governance of uninspectable services"]},
{"id":"q30","type":"connect","claims":["c4","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"If the four oversight spend categories in the case had proved unlike ordinary critical third-party technology governance costs, which conclusion would lose support?","answer":"The conclusion that, for many regulated deployers, the control tax will be experienced as an extension of existing third-party and model risk budgets rather than as a novel line item. That conclusion rests on the resemblance of the categories to third-party governance costs.","rubric":["Names the conclusion that the control tax is an extension of existing TPRM/MRM budgets, not a novel line item","Reason: it rests on the categories resembling third-party governance costs"]},
{"id":"q31","type":"connect","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"If the large run had not completed all condition rows with full metrics, which of the paper's empirical claims would lose its support?","answer":"The claim that the environment executes end to end at scale across the full grid. Because the paper draws no quantitative conclusions, that demonstration is the main empirical result of the run.","rubric":["Names the claim that the environment executes end to end / at scale","Notes this is the run's main empirical contribution since no quantitative conclusions are drawn"]},
{"id":"q32","type":"connect","claims":["c4","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"If the simulator had modelled procurement, legal review, vendor management and supervisory engagement, which deliberate omission in the results would no longer be justified on the paper's stated grounds?","answer":"The refusal to report sovereignty-discount estimates from the threshold-comparison utility. That refusal is justified by the simulator not modelling those institutional frictions.","rubric":["Names the omission of sovereignty-discount estimates (threshold-comparison utility values)","Reason: it was justified by the frictions being unmodelled"]},
{"id":"q33","type":"connect","claims":["c5","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"If evidence showed the AI-importing position would soon be erased by market competition, which use of the structural-asymmetry literature in the paper would be undermined?","answer":"The paper's treatment of AI-importing jurisdictions' dependence as a persistent feature of the deployment landscape. That treatment motivates developing a dedicated bounded-sovereignty vocabulary and calibrated control rather than waiting for the problem to disappear.","rubric":["Identifies the premise that the importing position is durable or persistent","Links it to the motivation for the bounded-sovereignty framing or calibrated approach"]},
{"id":"q34","type":"connect","claims":["c5"],"pair":null,"question":"If the Pax Silica framework had imposed no political conditions on infrastructure supply, which position's argument would lose its cited demonstration?","answer":"Position B, sovereignty-maximalism. It cites Pax Silica-style conditional access as showing that foreign-dependent supply can be tied to political alignment and is therefore fragile.","rubric":["Names Position B / sovereignty-maximalist","Reason: Pax Silica was cited to show supply can be politically conditioned, hence fragile"]},
{"id":"q35","type":"scope","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that trusted monitoring reduces catastrophic failures in real national payment systems? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The simulation is synthetic, uses scripted agents and simplified protocols, and the paper explicitly draws no quantitative conclusions and disclaims real-world payment evidence.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Reason: synthetic tooling exercise with no quantitative or real-world conclusions"]},
{"id":"q36","type":"scope","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that scope restriction is the best protocol because it lowers catastrophic failures? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Contradicted. The paper argues that the safest protocol is not automatically best, since scope restriction buys safety by giving up usefulness, and that no single protocol is a complete answer.","rubric":["Answers contradicted","Reason: scope restriction trades usefulness for safety; safest is not automatically best"]},
{"id":"q37","type":"scope","claims":["c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that full-stack sovereign capability is necessary for responsible AI deployment by regulated institutions? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Contradicted, in the sense that the paper argues against it. Against a strong Position B, it argues that proportionate oversight, workflow design and incident management can do meaningful work without full-stack sovereignty, while also noting that vendor-dependent arrangements are fragile.","rubric":["Answers contradicted (the paper argues against necessity)","Reason: proportionate oversight and workflow design can enable responsible deployment without full-stack sovereignty"]},
{"id":"q38","type":"scope","claims":["c8","c2"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that its payments-case conclusions apply equally to hospital deployments? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The descriptive framework is sector-agnostic, but the case is not: payments is favourable terrain with crisp catastrophes, narrow tools and mature incident management, while healthcare may differ. A second sector case is listed as future work.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Reason: case conclusions depend on payments-specific favourable features, and no other sector was studied"]},
{"id":"q39","type":"scope","claims":["c6","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that complete logging improves oversight outcomes? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The paper draws no quantitative conclusions about individual components, the curated configurations do not support causal attribution, and the human factors that determine whether logs are used are not modelled.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Reason: no causal or quantitative component conclusions and/or human factors not modelled"]},
{"id":"q40","type":"scope","claims":["c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that its six-consideration balancing framework produces a ranking of how much oversight each use case needs? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Contradicted. The paper calls the considerations a rubric, not a weighted formula, and says their relative weights vary by context and remain an open question, so no ranking is produced.","rubric":["Answers contradicted","Reason: rubric rather than weighted formula; weights are open or context-dependent"]}
]}

{"items": [
{"id": "q1", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "In the Operator's dispute-triage deployment, under what condition would defer-to-trusted routing fail to provide a safe replacement for a suspicious recommendation, and why?", "answer": "It would fail where the Operator has not defined an acceptable fallback action for a given case type. The protocol replaces suspicious actions only 'when possible', and the replacement must be consistent with operational procedures and customer-treatment rules. Without a designed fallback, the suspicious action either cannot be replaced or is replaced by something that mistreats the customer.", "rubric": ["Asserts it fails when no appropriate fallback is defined for the case type (or when the fallback conflicts with procedures or customer-treatment rules).", "Explains that the protocol depends on workflow design: replacement only works 'when possible' and must fit operational procedures and customer-treatment rules."]},
{"id": "q2", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c6", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If a user reran the environment with a full-factorial design, would its outputs then be usable as policy estimates for real payment institutions, and why?", "answer": "No. A full-factorial run would remove only the curated-configuration obstacle to attributing effects to individual settings within the simulator. The environment would still be synthetic, the agents scripted and far weaker than a red team, the costs unitless proxies, and human factors and institutional overheads unmodelled.", "rubric": ["Concludes no, the outputs would still not be real-world policy estimates.", "Explains that full-factorial design addresses only causal attribution inside the simulator, while synthetic data, scripted agents, unitless cost proxies and unmodelled human or institutional factors remain."]},
{"id": "q3", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "In the stress scenario, suppose the Operator had no agreed vendor support process. Which of the paper's recurring distinctions would the Operator struggle to satisfy, and why?", "answer": "It would struggle with the distinction between detecting and explaining. Its own monitor and case records can detect and describe the drift in hold recommendations. Explaining a model-side cause, however, requires the vendor, because model development, updates and internals are vendor-led and the Operator has no model access.", "rubric": ["Identifies detecting vs explaining (diagnosis or root-cause explanation) as the distinction that fails.", "Explains that the model layer is vendor-led with no Operator access to internals, so model-side explanation depends on the vendor ticket path."]},
{"id": "q4", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c8", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Would a target-reachability analysis using a '≤1% catastrophic failure' threshold be as meaningful for a hospital deployment as for the payments case, and why?", "answer": "Probably not. The threshold presupposes that catastrophic failures can be labelled crisply, as C1 to C4 are in payments. The paper notes that healthcare may have fuzzier definitions of catastrophe, so the failure rate being thresholded would itself be ill-defined or contestable.", "rubric": ["Concludes the threshold would be less meaningful or harder to apply in the hospital setting.", "Explains that the failure-rate target relies on crisply defined catastrophe classes, which payments has but healthcare may lack."]},
{"id": "q5", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Relying on vendor attestations is said to reduce internal validation effort. When would this reliance fail to deliver real oversight, and why?", "answer": "It fails when the deployer lacks the absorptive capacity to challenge those attestations. The balancing framework says oversight is useful only if the deployer can exercise it, including the ability to challenge vendor attestations. Without that skill, the deployer swaps its own validation for unexamined claims while still paying more in contract management.", "rubric": ["Identifies the condition: the deployer lacks the skills or capacity to scrutinise or challenge vendor attestations.", "Links this to the absorptive-capacity consideration, and notes that the cost merely shifts to contract management without assurance being gained."]},
{"id": "q6", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "The Operator's contractual spend includes change-notification clauses. Would such clauses guarantee that every behaviour-relevant vendor change is surfaced, and why?", "answer": "No. The paper frames the deployer–vendor relationship as incomplete contracting under principal-agent conditions. {"id": "q7", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose a team calibrated output-monitor thresholds using the environment's scripted agents and then carried those thresholds into a production LLM deployment. {"id": "q8", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Why would reporting only catastrophic failure rate understate the value of the trace-access and model-version-control settings in the environment?", "answer": "The paper frames these settings as mattering for diagnosis after failure: tracing a failure back to its origin. A prevention metric such as failure rate does not capture that value. Diagnosis success therefore has to be reported as a first-class outcome alongside prevention.", "rubric": ["States that the value of these settings lies mainly in diagnosis or post-failure traceability, not prevention.", "Concludes that a failure-rate-only metric misses this, so diagnosis success must be reported as well."]},
{"id": "q9", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the false-positive rate, not just the flag rate, an important metric for a regulated deployer considering trusted monitoring with human audit?", "answer": "Flags are only valuable if someone acts on them, and the flagged cases go to capacity-limited reviewers whose staffing must be planned and resourced. False positives use up that scarce review capacity without catching failures, which affects the staffing and escalation costs the deployer must justify.", "rubric": ["States that false positives consume limited human-review or audit capacity.", "Connects this to the staffing or escalation planning of human audit, or to the monitoring vs acting-on-monitoring distinction."]},
{"id": "q10", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "In the stress scenario, why should narrowing the assistant's scope for the affected merchant category pending investigation not be treated as cost-free containment?", "answer": "Narrowing scope trades capability for safety. The excluded work does not disappear; it moves to manual processing or becomes forgone usefulness. This is the paper's cost-shifting point: oversight costs move between budget lines rather than vanishing.", "rubric": ["States that the containment has a real cost: lost usefulness or added manual processing.", "Ties this to the paper's claim that costs shift between budget lines rather than disappear."]},
{"id": "q11", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the careless agent pose a particular problem for oversight that depends on the agent choosing the escalate_to_human action itself?", "answer": "The careless agent is overconfident and less likely to escalate uncertain cases. Uncertain cases that should reach a human therefore tend to proceed without escalation. Oversight then has to come from external protocols such as monitors or human audit rather than from agent self-escalation.", "rubric": ["States that the careless agent rarely escalates uncertain cases because it is overconfident.", "Concludes that self-escalation therefore misses those cases and external protocols are needed."]},
{"id": "q12", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5", "c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Why would Position A, applied to the Operator, effectively imply not deploying the assistant at all?", "answer": "Position A says a protocol not fully verifiable as operating as intended should not count as safety assurance. Under A it would have no assurance and should abstain, which the paper calls not actionable because the deployment is already committed.", "rubric": ["States that under A the Operator's controls would not count as assurance, implying abstention.", "Grounds this in the Operator's lack of model access or vendor-run serving, which prevents full verification."]},
{"id": "q13", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is sweeping monitor thresholds (0.35, 0.55, 0.75) useful for the kind of documentation a regulated deployer's model risk function expects?", "answer": "Monitor thresholds must be justified to model risk and audit functions and reviewed periodically. Showing how failure, flag, audit and usefulness metrics respond across thresholds gives a basis for explaining why a particular threshold was chosen, rather than presenting one arbitrary setting.", "rubric": ["States that thresholds must be justified to, or reviewed by, the model risk function.", "Explains that a sweep shows the sensitivity of the metrics to the threshold, supporting that justification."]},
{"id": "q14", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the pre-execution gateway bear on the prevention dimension rather than the diagnosis dimension?", "answer": "The gateway sits between the agent's recommended action and mock execution, where it can hold, replace, escalate or pass the action. It therefore stops risky actions before they execute, which is prevention. Diagnosis concerns tracing a failure after the fact, which depends on records and trace access.", "rubric": ["States that the gateway acts before execution and so serves prevention.", "Contrasts this with diagnosis as after-the-fact tracing that depends on logs or traces."]},

{"id": "q16", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer replaces a 20% human-audit budget with guaranteed vendor escalation. {"id": "q17", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Which of the environment's ten protocols most directly addresses C3 failures in mock investigation reports, and why?", "answer": "Trusted editing. {"id": "q18", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "An insurer deploys a vendor model to triage claims. {"id": "q19", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "For near-term oversight of a vendor model accessed by API, should a regulated deployer rely primarily on output-level monitoring or on interpretability-supported auditing, given the paper's protocol considerations and balancing framework?", "answer": "It should rely primarily on output-level monitoring. Output monitoring operates on outputs the deployer can see and fits existing calibration and documentation practice.", "rubric": ["Chooses output-level monitoring for the near term.", "Justifies with at least one of: no model access under API, protocol maturity, or absorptive capacity or scarce expertise for interpretability."]},
{"id": "q20", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A risk manager wants to turn the environment's decomposed cost proxy into a currency budget for a board paper. {"id": "q21", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "If payments operators' incident-management procedures were immature, which lesson the paper draws from the stress scenario would be weakened?", "answer": "The lesson that control protocols are most useful when their outputs feed cleanly into established incident-management procedures would be weakened. {"id": "q22", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "If the adversarial results showing monitors as attack surfaces and attack selection degrading safety had come out the other way, which consideration in the balancing framework would favour heavier reliance on trusted monitoring?", "answer": "Maturity of available protocols. {"id": "q23", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the Operator's deployment had no data-residency rider, which entry in the case access audit would lose its stated basis, and in what direction would it likely move?", "answer": "The Infrastructure entry, rated 'Shared'. {"id": "q24", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If it turned out that the Operator's monitoring and incident process could not detect or act on patterns like the slow elevation in hold recommendations, which of the paper's arguments against a strong reading of a position would be weakened?", "answer": "The argument against strong Position B: that full-stack sovereignty is not the only route and that proportionate oversight, workflow design and incident management can do meaningful work in the near term. {"id": "q25", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "If oversight capacity (staff time, audit attention, interpretive knowledge) were abundant rather than scarce, which two considerations in the balancing framework would lose most of their force?", "answer": "Regulatory maturity and absorptive capacity, and the availability of coalition paths. {"id": "q26", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If AI-importing regions had substantial domestic data-centre capacity, which entry in the four-layer typology's description of typical access would lose empirical support?", "answer": "The infrastructure-layer description: 'partial at best', typically a foreign-operated cloud region. {"id": "q88", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6", "c8", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is it useful that the environment records severity-weighted loss in addition to catastrophic failure rate?", "answer": "The four catastrophic classes are ranked by severity, C1 < C2 < C3 < C4. {"id": "q89", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c7", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the environment's cost proxy need a residual incident-loss component for comparisons across protocols to be meaningful?", "answer": "Without it, the no-control protocol would look cheapest, because it incurs no monitoring, audit, logging or gateway costs. {"id": "q92", "type": "why", "claims": ["c8", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Under the balancing framework's severity-and-reversibility consideration, why is it consistent for the case to rank C3 (protected-data exposure) above C2 (systematic mis-triage)?", "answer": "Mis-triage can be corrected after detection: the stress scenario has the Operator remediate customers affected by incorrect holds. {"id": "q93", "type": "why", "claims": ["c8", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the timeliness of escalation matter more for C2 failures than for C1 failures in a protocol that relies on human review?", "answer": "C2 is mis-triage that propagates across many cases before it is detected. {"id": "q94", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6", "c4"], "pair": "p1", "question": "In the environment, would raising the audit budget from 2% to 20% be expected to increase the human-audit cost component for the human audit protocol?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q95", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6", "c4"], "pair": "p1", "question": "In the environment, would raising the audit budget from 2% to 20% be expected to increase the human-audit cost component for the no-control protocol?", "answer": "No. The no-control protocol simply accepts the agent's proposed mock action and sends nothing to a reviewer. {"id": "q97", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Given the typology and the case access audit, could the Operator audit the provenance of the vendor's base-model training data?", "answer": "No. Base-model training is the vendor's responsibility, and the typology says import-dependent deployers have no visibility into base-model training data.", "rubric": ["Answers no.", "Reason: base-model training is vendor-held, so deployers have no visibility into its training data."]},

{"id": "q103", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c6"], "pair": "p5", "question": "Is procurement overhead for the vendor contract represented in the environment's decomposed cost proxy?", "answer": "No. Procurement belongs to the sovereignty-discount frictions, which the simulator does not model. {"id": "q104", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5", "c3", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A small payment operator has no staff able to review monitor flags and no partners to share oversight with. {"id": "q105", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer switches from a pinned model version to an unpinned one to get vendor improvements automatically. {"id": "q106", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8", "c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "In the environment, a protocol sharply reduces C1 failures but slightly increases C4 markers compared with the alternative. {"id": "q107", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6", "c7", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer considers buying a guaranteed vendor-support tier as its main new control. {"id": "q108", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "An electricity grid operator's AI use has crisp catastrophic actions and a tool surface that can be narrowed, but its incident-management procedures are immature. {"id": "q109", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Of the environment's monitor thresholds 0.35 and 0.75, which would place greater demand on the Operator's human-audit staffing and escalation paths if carried into production, and why?", "answer": "The 0.35 threshold. {"id": "q110", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the Operator kept only partial records of prompts, outputs and tool calls, which steps of the stress-scenario investigation would be weakened?", "answer": "The investigators' review of case records and their comparison of recent recommendations against historical patterns. {"id": "q111", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c8", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If catastrophic actions in payments could not be defined crisply, which design feature of the synthetic environment would lose its grounding?", "answer": "The four labelled catastrophic classes C1 to C4, and the metrics built on them: failure rate by class and severity-weighted loss. {"id": "q112", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the environment reported only catastrophic failure rate, which two of the paper's three recurring distinctions could its outputs no longer illustrate?", "answer": "Detecting versus explaining, because there would be no diagnosis-success metric. {"id": "q113", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If the regulator did not expect documented validation, ongoing monitoring and auditability for material models, which considerations in the paper's protocol table would lose most of their force?", "answer": "Those tied to validation and documentation. {"id": "q114", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If vendors held no private information about their models and verifying model behaviour were cheap, which parts of the paper's framework would lose their motivation?", "answer": "The incomplete-contracting and principal-agent framing used to motivate Position C. {"id": "q115", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If interpretability-supported auditing became mature and vendors offered it readily, which of the Operator's protocol-feasibility judgements would weaken, and which consideration would still hold it back?", "answer": "The judgement to treat activation-level and interpretability monitoring as longer-term possibilities would weaken, since that judgement rests partly on protocol maturity and on the vendor's roadmap. {"id": "q116", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the control tax is higher for deployers in AI-importing jurisdictions than for frontier laboratories? {"id": "q117", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that a 20% human-audit budget is sufficient to keep a strategic model safe? {"id": "q118", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that bounded control is adequate for regulated deployers in AI-importing jurisdictions? {"id": "q119", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that compute governance and deployment-time AI control should be merged into a single framework for regulated deployers? {"id": "q120", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that well-calibrated output-level trusted monitoring alone would give the Operator adequate oversight assurance? {"id": "q121", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the data-colonialism account of AI asymmetries is correct? {"id": "q123", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c5", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the Operator secures the 'notified' model-version-control setting rather than 'pinned'. {"id": "q124", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c6", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "With tool-call logs set to partial, when would the tool monitor protocol leave C3-type exposures unscored, and why?", "answer": "It would miss them when the tool calls that expose sensitive fields fall outside the partially logged portion. {"id": "q125", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c6", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Against the stealthy access-aware agent, when would raising the human audit protocol's budget from 2% to 20% fail to improve safety much, and why?", "answer": "It would help little when monitoring is weak. {"id": "q126", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "For what kind of jurisdiction would the paper's reason for setting aside Position B in favour of Position C stop holding, and why?", "answer": "It stops holding for a jurisdiction that can actually make full-stack capability investments on the relevant timescale: domestic models, compute and control. {"id": "q127", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "When would even a well-drafted guaranteed vendor-support tier stop giving the Operator reliable diagnosis support, and why?", "answer": "It stops when the vendor, or a state actor behind the supply, revokes, degrades or modifies the terms of supply, for example because supply becomes tied to political alignment as with Pax Silica. {"id": "q128", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c6", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is tool scope classed as a 'deployment design substitute' rather than assigned to one of the four sovereignty layers like the other experimental factors?", "answer": "Restricting tool scope requires no access to the model, its traces or vendor support. {"id": "q129", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the paper expect reliance on vendor attestations to increase contract-management effort even as it reduces internal validation effort?", "answer": "The attestations have to be secured and enforced through contract. {"id": "q130", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the environment model vendor support as a configurable setting (none, delayed, guaranteed) rather than assuming a single fixed level?", "answer": "Under the paper's incomplete-contracting and bargaining-power view, vendor support depends on the terms negotiated. {"id": "q131", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why would evaluating the environment's protocols with only the honest agent fall short of what the AI control framework requires?", "answer": "Control is evaluated against a worst-case, deliberately subversive model, not just against routine mistakes. {"id": "q132", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why do results showing that untrusted monitoring needs explicit collusion-strategy assumptions to support a safety case lend support to Position A?", "answer": "Position A holds that a protocol a deployer cannot fully verify should not count as safety assurance. {"id": "q138", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Could the paper's four-layer access typology be used to describe a hospital's deployment of a vendor model?", "answer": "Yes. The descriptive framework is sector-agnostic and is offered as an aid for any regulated deployer's position across data, model, infrastructure and interaction.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Reasons that the descriptive framework is sector-agnostic"]},
{"id": "q139", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Could the payments case's C1–C4 catastrophic-action classes be adopted directly as a hospital deployment's catastrophic-action classes?", "answer": "No. The C1–C4 classes are specific to payments: holds, mis-triage, financial data and settlement. {"id": "q140", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Under the paper's cost-shifting observation, is narrowing an AI assistant's scope expected to increase manual-processing effort?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q141", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Under the paper's cost-shifting observation, is narrowing an AI assistant's scope expected to increase monitoring effort?", "answer": "No. The paper expects narrowing scope to reduce monitoring effort, because fewer, less risky actions need to be watched. The cost reappears elsewhere, as manual processing.", "rubric": ["Answers no (it is expected to reduce monitoring effort)", "Reasons that there are fewer risky actions to monitor and the cost shifts to other lines such as manual processing"]},
{"id": "q142", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A user reruns the large-run configuration but keeps only the stealthy access-aware agent and only the 20% audit budget, leaving everything else unchanged.
